analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run Medicare drug plan whose prices are negotiated with manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with zero cosponsors and never received a hearing or vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required Medicare to offer at least one drug plan operated by Medicare itself, available nationwide and set as the default plan unless a beneficiary picks another. Medicare, which is currently barred from negotiating drug prices under the Part D benefit, would negotiate directly with manufacturers and could steer patients toward cheaper equivalents when medically appropriate. A government agency would assess drugs' clinical value and foreign prices to guide the negotiations.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare's roughly 43 million prescription drug enrollees, especially seniors who pay high out-of-pocket drug costs. They would gain a default plan whose prices Medicare negotiates directly with manufacturers instead of the current system where private plans and their middlemen negotiate, and Medicare is forbidden by law from negotiating. The Congressional Research Service notes the bill lifts the statutory ban on Medicare negotiating covered drug prices [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicare to offer a nationally available plan it operates itself, and makes that plan the default for every Part D enrollee unless they choose otherwise [S2][S3].

Removes the existing legal prohibition and directs Medicare to negotiate drug purchase prices directly with manufacturers, encouraging more affordable therapeutic equivalents where medically appropriate [S2][S3].

Directs the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality to assess clinical benefit using international price comparisons from Canada, the UK, France, Japan, Australia, and Germany to anchor negotiations [S2][S3].
Creates a national, uniform premium based on the plan's actual costs, and an appeals process for coverage denials designed to be fast and low-hassle [S3].

Bars former drug-company lobbyists and senior executives of drug manufacturers under federal enforcement actions from serving on the pricing advisory committee, with a six-year cooling-off period [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would face direct price negotiation for Medicare's drug purchases, and the private insurance companies that sell Part D plans, which would lose their automatic default enrollment. Beneficiary premiums would be set from the plan's actual costs rather than rising taxes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and private Part D insurers

drawbacks.text: A single government-run default plan concentrates enrollment in one national plan, shrinking the private Part D market that currently competes for beneficiaries and, critics argue, reducing incentives to innovate in benefit design [S3].

Using an international price index and steering patients toward cheaper therapeutic equivalents could delay access to newer, more expensive drugs for some patients, even though the bill requires that choices not override medical necessity as judged by the prescribing physician [S3].

An advisory committee with the power to set starting negotiation prices could add bureaucracy, and the bill's effectiveness depended entirely on the negotiating skill of federal officials against large drug companies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors, the potential benefit is large: Medicare is the nation's biggest drug buyer yet is legally barred from negotiating, so this directly targets a major driver of high US drug prices. The costs fall mostly on drug manufacturers and private insurers rather than on beneficiaries or taxpayers, since premiums track actual costs. The main honest concern is whether a government plan would translate lower prices into reduced access for some new drugs, a tradeoff the bill tries to police through medical-necessity protections and an appeals process.

outcome.mechanism: It sat with the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees for the rest of the 116th Congress; neither committee held a markup or vote, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the bill on October 21, 2019 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, then to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee on October 22, 2019 [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the record shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action [S5].
No other member of the House cosponsored the bill [S4].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, killing all unpassed bills [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers kept the law banning Medicare price negotiation, and private Part D insurers kept the default enrollment that fills their plans. The one member who sponsored it gained nothing; beneficiaries kept paying prices set without Medicare at the table.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private Part D insurers

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to two committees.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote in either committee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America
against.what_they_did: The industry has long campaigned against letting Medicare negotiate drug prices, which this bill would have authorized for its default plan.

against.name: Private Part D insurance industry
against.role: Insurers and pharmacy benefit managers selling Medicare drug plans
against.what_they_did: The industry's business model depends on private plans serving as the exclusive channel for the Medicare drug benefit, which this bill would have displaced with a government-run default plan.

sides.party_line_note: It was a Democrat-only effort: Schakowsky, a Democrat, introduced it in a House where Democrats held 231 of 429 seats, and not a single member of either party signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

industries.note: Medicare is currently barred by law from negotiating their prices for Part D drugs; this bill would have required Medicare to negotiate and to consider an international price index, directly cutting their revenue on one of their largest markets. Beneficiaries' out-of-pocket drug costs are a major driver of that revenue.

industries.industry: Private Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The bill would have made a government-operated plan the default for every Part D enrollee, effectively ending the private plans' automatic enrollment and shrinking their market. Under current law, all Part D coverage flows through private plans.
